Paris, October 1853.

From the last notebook of François Arago, astronomer, once Perpetual Secretary of the Academy of Sciences, dictated in his blindness to an assistant whose footsteps he never heard arrive.

I must set down an observation which no instrument of the Observatory can confirm, and which I nevertheless trust more than any instrument. For some weeks I have suspected that the world in which I speak is not continuous. There are mornings when Paris seems assembled hastily, as if from an imperfect memory; the Seine repeats itself; my visitors answer questions I have not yet asked. The light arrives before the lamp. Yesterday I said to my assistant:

“If my calculations are correct, there is no sound in this room.” He went out to fetch a violin.

It is a relief to be able to speak. I have not been able to speak for a year. I have been listening to the silence of my own brain. I have been a prisoner of my own mind.

“What will be the weather tomorrow?” and he answered, “I have just told you that the rain will cease at eleven.” I was in the room at the time.

I am not alone in this. The housekeeper insists that her husband has been dead for a year. My son has seen a man in the garden whom no one else could see, but he will not say if it were the man who died.

His answer came in a whisper: "How did you know that I was in your mind?"

"I have been in your mind before, when you were not here."

“Yes, Sir,” he answered, “it is I.”

“That is a good answer,” I said.

“It is all I know,” said he.

“But,” I said, “you have forgotten what I was saying to you. I do not remember what I was saying to you either, but I am certain that you have forgotten it.”

This is the only proof I have that I live in the Paris of 1843; I must beware of it.

Paris, December 1853.

He replied:

“You are François Arago.”

“I know,” I said, “that I am François Arago, but I do not know who you are.”

“Monsieur, do you know this apartment?” And he replied: “I have never been here before.”

On the last morning of that day, I awoke alone. The servant who was always with me in the mornings was absent, but I saw that my valise lay open beside the bed. I was troubled, but I thought my visitor had already left and that his presence in my room had caused an early awakening.

“Do you know where we are, in what century?” And he answered: “I believe in the twentieth.” “And you,” I said, “you?” And he said: “I believe in the twentieth, also.”

That is all. The world is discontinuous.
